reasoning:
The finding's load-bearing claim is false. It asserts: "NIOHTTP1 writes the URI verbatim into the request line — .build/checkouts/swift-nio/Sources/NIOHTTP1/HTTPEncoder.swift:719-726, swift-nio 2.101.3, no validation." The analyst read the encoder but never opened the handler that sits in front of it.

CONTROL NOT OPENED — NIO installs a request-target allow-list by default.

1. All four transports set up the pipeline with a zero-argument call: /Users/joshlacalamito/Developer/Catbird+Petrel/Swan/Sources/SwanOAuth/NIOPeerPinnedOAuthDocumentTransport.swift:91 `try channel.pipeline.syncOperations.addHTTPClientHandlers()` (same at SwanProxyHTTPTransport.swift:284, NIOPeerPinnedOAuthPostTransport.swift:162, SwanAccounts/NIOPeerPinnedATHandleHTTPTransport.swift:114). Swan never passes `enableOutboundHeaderValidation: false` anywhere.

2. Every public `addHTTPClientHandlers` overload on `SynchronousOperations` — including the older one at .build/checkouts/swift-nio/Sources/NIOHTTP1/HTTPPipelineSetup.swift:450-460 that has no `enableOutboundHeaderValidation` parameter at all — funnels into the private `_addHTTPClientHandlers` at HTTPPipelineSetup.swift:643-650, whose `enableOutboundHeaderValidation: Bool = true` (line 646) is the default. Both branches insert the validator: fast path at :684 `let requestHeaderValidator = NIOHTTPRequestHeadersValidator()`, fallback at :707-709. There is no overload reachable from a bare `addHTTPClientHandlers()` that omits it.

3. `NIOHTTPRequestHeadersValidator` is a `ChannelOutboundHandler` that validates the URI, not just headers: .build/checkouts/swift-nio/Sources/NIOHTTP1/HTTPHeaderValidator.swift:34 `guard Self.uriOnlyContainsAllowedCharacters(head.uri), ...` else `promise?.fail(HTTPParserError.invalidHeaderToken)` and `return` WITHOUT calling `context.write` (:36-40). `uriOnlyContainsAllowedCharacters` (:54-127) is a byte allow-list of exactly ALPHA / DIGIT / `-._~` / gen-delims / sub-delims / `%`. Its own comment at :96-98 states the intent verbatim: "Everything outside this set — SP, CTLs (%x00-1F / %x7F), non-ASCII ... MUST be percent-encoded. Bare CR, LF, or NUL in the request-target MUST be rejected (request smuggling / response splitting)."

4. Ordering puts the validator BEFORE the encoder on the outbound path. HTTPPipelineSetup.swift:685-688 adds `[requestEncoder, ByteToMessageHandler(responseDecoder), requestHeaderValidator]` at `.last`, so the validator is the tail-most of the three. The only handler added after it (`OAuthDocumentResponseHandler`, NIOPeerPinnedOAuthDocumentTransport.swift:92-100) is `ChannelInboundHandler` only. Outbound writes originate at the tail, so `try await channel.writeAndFlush(HTTPClientRequestPart.head(head)).get()` at NIOPeerPinnedOAuthDocumentTransport.swift:134 hits the validator first; a decoded CR/LF fails the promise and that `.get()` throws before `HTTPRequestEncoder.write(request:)` ever runs. Zero bytes reach the socket. Confirmed against the resolved version: Package.resolved pins swift-nio 2.101.3, which is the checkout read above.

Consequence: the exact PoC in the finding cannot work. `%0d%0aX-Injected:%20yes` decodes to CR, LF and SP — all three are outside the allow-list, and any injected header needs at least one of them. There is no request-line injection, no header injection, and no pipelined second request. The high-severity framing does not survive.

The sibling transport's `uri.utf8.allSatisfy { (0x21...0x7E).contains($0) }` at SwanProxyHTTPTransport.swift:227-229 is therefore defense-in-depth layered over an existing NIO control, not the sole protection — and its own comment at :215-217 justifies itself purely in terms of path rewriting ("would silently rewrite an encoded path segment"), never mentioning CRLF, which is consistent with the author knowing NIO already polices the charset.

WHAT ACTUALLY REMAINS is a much smaller bug. Bytes inside NIO's allow-list still decode through `url.path`: `%2F`→`/`, `%3F`→`?`, `%23`→`#`, `%3A`→`:`, `%25`→`%`, sub-delims. So `https://h/a%2Fb` is fetched as `/a/b` — a same-origin request-target rewrite. Its impact is further bounded by OAuthClientMetadata.swift:241-246 `validateResponseIdentity`, which requires the fetched document's `client_id` to equal the requested URL string byte-for-byte, so metadata confusion is blocked. That is a correctness/hygiene defect deserving the one-line `components.percentEncodedPath` change for consistency with the sibling — not a high-severity unauthenticated CRLF-injection vulnerability on a live production PDS, and it does not justify the proposed multi-file change plus extracted helper plus new test suite.

Uncertainty noted and checked: the constraint that Linux x86_64 (swift:6.1-jammy) is authoritative does not rescue the finding — the entire control is platform-independent Swift in swift-nio, not Foundation. The `url.path` percent-decoding premise itself is not in dispute; it is the step from "decoded CR/LF in the target String" to "CRLF on the wire" that is refuted.

I could not refute it. I opened every link and found no earlier gate, no unobtainable precondition, no safe-behavior test, and no documented intent.

Strongest single piece of evidence that it is real — the charge/refund asymmetry across the WebSocket upgrade:

`.build/checkouts/hummingbird/Sources/HummingbirdCore/Server/AvailableConnectionsHandler.swift:100-113` charges on accept (`self.delegate.connectionOpened()` in `channelRead`) and refunds only from `channel.closeFuture...whenComplete { values.handler.delegate.connectionClosed() }`; :116-121 `read(context:)` returns WITHOUT calling `context.read()` once `isAcceptingNewConnections()` is false, and `MaximumAvailableConnections.isAcceptingNewConnections()` is exactly `connectionCount < maxConnections` (:59-61). A WebSocket upgrade reuses the same child channel and never closes it, so an idle subscriber holds its slot for its whole lifetime. The delegate is installed on the public listener at Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanHTTP.swift:1130-1136 with `configuration.maximumConnections`, default 256 at :132, and `swan serve` constructs the configuration as `.init(host:port:publicURL:publicRouteSurface:)` (Sources/swan/SwanCommand.swift:3040-3045) — it never passes the value, and no `--max-connections` flag exists in Sources/swan. So 256 anonymous responsive-idle sockets halt accept for every public route.

Two corrections to their framing that do NOT refute the finding:
1. "Total loss of the listener" overstates slightly — the management surface is a SEPARATE `Application` with its own `MaximumAvailableConnections(configuration.maximumConnections)` defaulting to 32 (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanManagementHTTP.swift:36, 440-441), so admin endpoints survive. Everything on the public listener (login, OAuth, public reads, permissioned routes, relay reconnect) does not.
2. Exhaustion halts `context.read()` on the accept channel, so new TCP connections queue in the kernel backlog rather than being reset; already-established connections (including the relay's live subscription) keep working. The federation impact is on reconnect, which is what they claimed.

Their sub-claim triage matches my independent read: (a) auto-ping genuinely does evict non-reading clients; (b) responsive-idle is the unmitigated core; (c) the post-hoc `maximumWriteDuration` measurement at PublicFirehoseStreaming.swift:228-233 is a real defect with uncertain exploitation on today's small retained window; (d) fan-out is 256 non-blocking `continuation.yield` calls into 1-slot buffers, not meaningfully O(N) work; (e) the 0.25 s poll is arithmetically real but minor.

Two scope corrections that do not rescue the finding: OAuthBlockingDNSAdmission.shared is 4 permits and fail-fast (OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:193-215), so a DNS-stalling variant partly self-limits and the attacker's best play is fast DNS plus a silent TCP peer (~5s/slot, 8 slots, ~1.6 req/s); and separately SystemOAuthHostnameResolver.queue (:347) is a SERIAL DispatchQueue whose in-flight getaddrinfo cannot be cancelled (:252-258), so one blackholed-DNS client_id pins all OAuth DNS process-wide from a single request — a cheaper adjacent variant that belongs in the same remediation. Severity is availability-only (transient, self-healing, one real account, which may not use OAuth daily), so "high" is arguable, but the mechanism, unauthenticated reachability, and /oauth/token blast radius all hold as stated.

Strongest single piece of evidence that it is real: the freshness row is committed with a 3600 s retention and counted against the 8,192 cap BEFORE any validation, and no release path exists anywhere in Sources. Concretely, Sources/SwanOAuth/OAuthClientMetadataLoader.swift:286-294 awaits `controlStore.beginClientMetadataFetch` and only then, at :296, calls `admittedFetcher.fetchJSON`; `beginClientMetadataFetch` (Sources/SwanSQLite/OAuthControlStore.swift:398-415) commits `issueClientMetadataFetchTicketLocked` (:1224-1288), which checks `requireInsertionCapacity(... maximumRows: oauthControlStorageLimits.clientMetadataFreshness)` (:1230-1234; `.production` = 8_192 at :116-117) and upserts `retain_until = now + clientMetadataFreshnessRetention` (=3_600, :201) with `MAX(existing, excluded)` (:1268-1281). A grep for `oauth_control_client_metadata_freshness` across Sources/ returns exactly three writers: that insert, the success-only UPDATE in `markClientMetadataFetchPublishedLocked` (:1301), and the DELETE in `purgeExpiredLocked` (:1529-1541) which requires BOTH `freshness.retain_until <= now` AND `metadata.client_id IS NULL`. So a ticket whose fetch fails at :296 / decode fails at :299 / JWKS fails at :307 leaves a row that is un-deletable for a full hour, and `requireInsertionCapacity` (:1197-1222) then throws SwanError.unavailable for every client_id without an existing row.

Refutation routes tried and why each failed:
1. Earlier allow-list or costly precondition on client_id — `OAuthClientMetadata.validateStandardClientID` (Sources/SwanOAuth/OAuthClientMetadata.swift:331) is just `validateHTTPSClientID` (:335-342): https scheme, host non-nil, no port/user/password/fragment. Path and query are unconstrained, so 8,192 distinct client_ids come from one hostname. And because DNS resolution plus `policy.validateURL` happen inside `fetchJSONWithoutAdmission` (OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:552-560), i.e. after the ticket, the hostname need not even resolve.
2. Route-level admission or rate limiting — the PAR handler (Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanOAuthAuthorizationServerHTTP.swift:164, body :180-296) has no rate limiter; the only pre-load control is a DPoP proof at :212-230, which is attacker-self-signed after one nonce-challenge round trip, and it precedes `clientMetadataLoader.load` at :233. `OAuthRemoteFetchAdmission.acquire` (OAuthRemoteFetch.swift:485-495) and `maximumConcurrentFlights = 8` (OAuthClientMetadataLoader.swift:86) bound concurrency only, never cumulative row count.
3. Not reachable on the deployed configuration — docker-compose.yml:98 passes `--enable-oauth-authorization-server`, exactly the flag that builds the loader and AS configuration (Sources/swan/SwanCommand.swift:2442-2447 and 2492-2515). Memory of live PAR nonce challenges on swan.place corroborates the route is publicly reachable.
4. Existing test asserting the safe behaviour — Tests/SwanSQLiteTests/OAuthControlStorageHardeningTests.swift asserts only the fail-closed cap; nothing tests ticket release after a failed fetch, and no `abandon`-style API is declared in Sources/SwanStorage/SwanStorage.swift:522-533 (only begin/publish).
5. Deliberate documented contract — the only documented intent near the code (OAuthControlStore.swift:450-453) is about publication ordering (highest published generation wins), which the proposed abandon guards preserve; nothing documents pre-validation allocation with 1 h retention as intended. The codebase in fact already uses the compensating-release idiom elsewhere: `abandonPublicRepositoryReservation` (Sources/SwanStorage/PublicRepositoryStore.swift:105) invoked from Sources/SwanHTTP/SwanPublicRepositoryMutationCoordinator.swift:67,70,202,205.

One correction that strengthens rather than weakens the finding: the analyst's severity note relies on the 300 s metadata cache, but the token endpoint calls `configuration.clientMetadataLoader.revalidate(clientID:)` unconditionally on every grant (SwanOAuthAuthorizationServerHTTP.swift:540, with the deliberate comment at :537-539), and `revalidate` sets `bypassCache: true` (OAuthClientMetadataLoader.swift:349-351), skipping the cache and always allocating a ticket. `/oauth/revoke` does the same at :645. So on a poisoned-full table the single real account's token refresh — not merely new client onboarding — fails with 503 `temporarily_unavailable` as soon as its freshness row lapses.

Note on the fix: item 3 is consistent with the `MAX(existing, excluded)` upsert at OAuthControlStore.swift:1272-1277, so a short initial retention cannot shorten an already-published client's row.
